title: Christmas Pageant Lantern Bid
subject: Contracts
stem:
Esther, a general event contractor, was preparing a sealed bid for Lydia’s private Christmas Pageant Pavilion. Paul, a lighting installer, sent Esther this signed email:

Will install all overhead lantern trusses and speaker wiring for the pavilion, per Lydia’s specifications, for $32,000 if you accept within a reasonable time after the prime contract is awarded.
/s/ Paul

Ruth, Stephen, and Barnabas sent similar sub-bids of $40,000, $42,000, and $44,000. Esther used Paul’s $32,000 figure in preparing and submitting her own sealed bid to Lydia. Before the bids were opened, Paul truthfully told Esther that his sub-bid had been based on an $8,000 computational error and was therefore revoked. Shortly afterward, Lydia awarded Esther the pavilion contract. Esther then contracted with Ruth to do the lighting work for $40,000. Esther sues Paul to recover $8,000.

Which of the following, if proved, would most strengthen Esther’s prospect of recovery?
call: Which of the following, if proved, would most strengthen Esther's prospect of recovery?

choices.A: Paul was negligent in erroneously calculating the amount of his sub-bid.
choices.B: After Paul's notice of revocation, Esther made a reasonable effort to subcontract with another lighting installer at the lowest possible price.
choices.C: Lydia had required Esther to submit a bid bond, and Esther could not have withdrawn or amended her prime bid without forfeiting that bond.
choices.D: Esther dealt with all of her subcontractors in good faith and without seeking to renegotiate lower prices they had bid.

rightExplanation:
C most strengthens Esther’s recovery.

Gold Key: A subcontractor’s bid can become temporarily irrevocable when the subcontractor should expect the general contractor to rely on it in a prime bid and the contractor is locked into that reliance before acceptance.

Silver Key: In a “most strengthens recovery” array, pick the fact that supplies the missing legal link. C supplies that link. The bid bond means Esther could not withdraw or amend her own prime bid without a real forfeiture. That makes her use of Paul’s bid a locked-in reliance fact, not just a business inconvenience.

c3.label: CUT
c3.text:
Use the Gold Key first. The needed fact is not “who behaved well later” or “who made the mistake.” The needed fact is “why the sub-bid was temporarily irrevocable.”

* A cuts as NOT_RESPONSIVE / wrong_element. It proves fault, not lock-in reliance.
* B cuts as NOT_RESPONSIVE / wrong_element. It proves mitigation, not temporary irrevocability.
* D cuts as NOT_RESPONSIVE / wrong_element. It proves general fair dealing, not the legal lock-in fact.

c3.label: CLASH
c3.text: No two true-and-responsive choices remain after the anchor-assisted cut. The apparent tension is “collateral helpful fact” versus “missing legal link.”

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: C is the residual. It gives the bid bond and no-withdrawal fact.

studentScript: C. I need the fact that makes the sub-bid stay open. Bid bond plus no withdrawal is the lock-in fact; mitigation, negligence, and general good faith do not create the recovery right.

A.signal: A talks about Paul's math fault; it does not show Esther was trapped in her own bid before acceptance.
A.lawyer: Negligent calculation does not by itself establish the temporary irrevocability of the sub-bid under reliance doctrine.

B.signal: B happens after revocation and helps the substitute-price story; it does not explain why Paul's offer stayed open.
B.lawyer: Mitigation can bear on damages amount, but the key liability issue is whether reliance made the sub-bid temporarily irrevocable.

C.signal: C supplies the missing bridge; Esther could not undo the prime bid without forfeiting the bond.
C.lawyer: The bid bond/no-withdrawal fact supports substantial reliance and injustice, making the sub-bid temporarily irrevocable.

D.signal: D shows clean dealing in general; it still does not show Esther was bound to her prime bid when Paul revoked.
D.lawyer: No bid shopping may prevent a separate unfairness objection, but it is not the strongest fact proving temporary irrevocability.

goldKeys.statement: A subcontractor bid can become temporarily irrevocable when the subcontractor should expect the general contractor to rely on it in a prime bid and the contractor is locked into that reliance before acceptance.
goldKeys.trigger: A low subcontractor bid is used in a sealed prime bid, then the subcontractor revokes before the prime contract is awarded.
goldKeys.unlocks: The bid-bond fact supplies the missing lock-in link; mitigation, fault, and general good faith do not.
goldKeys.authority: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §87(2); Drennan v. Star Paving Co., 51 Cal. 2d 409 (1958).

silverKeys.statement: On a 'most strengthens recovery' array, first identify the missing legal link. A fact that locks the claimant into reliance beats facts about later mitigation, fault, or general fairness.
silverKeys.trigger: The choices are all helpful-sounding facts, but only one explains why the revoked offer stayed open.
silverKeys.unlocks: The array tempts students to pick the responsible damages fact instead of the fact that creates the right to recover.

remediation.title: Sub-bid recovery needs lock-in reliance
remediation.signal: Low sub-bid used in prime bid, then revoked before award.
remediation.studentMove: Find the fact that shows the general contractor was locked into the prime bid.
